name: Personal H2S (hydrogen sulphide) monitors
summary: A matchbox-sized clip-on alarm with one electrochemical sensor that beeps, flashes and vibrates when hydrogen sulphide reaches its set level in ppm.
uses: Warns of H2S, which your nose can't track: smell is lost at 100 to 150 ppm, and 700 to 1,000 ppm drops people in 1 or 2 breaths (OSHA H2S)
Measures H2S only, not oxygen, flammable gas, CO or CO2 (BW CLIP); the CDC oil-tank deaths studied were from hydrocarbon vapour and low oxygen, with H2S ruled out (MMWR TANKS)
Default alarms of 10 and 15 ppm sit above ACGIH's 1 ppm (8 hours) and 5 ppm (short-term); many Canadian jurisdictions have similar limits (BW CLIP, CCOHS H2S)
An alarm means leave the area at once; it isn't a safe level to keep working in (MSA 4XR)
Range tops out (0 to 100 ppm on a BW Clip), and a big dose can leave the sensor needing hours to recover (BW CLIP, MSA 4XR)
identify: About the size of a matchbox, clipped to a collar, chest pocket or hard hat, with a grille over the sensor, bright flashers and a horn (95 dB on a BW Clip) (BW CLIP). Makers colour-code: Honeywell's BW Clip is labelled yellow for H2S, grey for CO, light grey for O2 (BW CLIP). Other common ones: MSA Altair, Industrial Scientific Tango, Dräger Pac, Honeywell ToxiRAE. Some disposable types don't show a running gas level: a basic BW Clip can show the level only during an alarm, while the Real Time model shows ppm all the time (BW CLIP). Units are ppm. Common default alarms are low 10, high 15 ppm (BW CLIP, MSA 4XR); MSA's low-range H2S sensor uses 5 and 10 with a 1 ppm 8-hour average (MSA 4XR). ACGIH's limits are 1 ppm over 8 hours and 5 ppm short-term (CCOHS H2S), so a monitor that stays quiet at 9 ppm is not saying the air is harmless. Alarm points can be changed, so check the label or menu. Marks listed on a BW Clip: cULus Class I Division 1, ATEX and IECEx Ex ia (BW CLIP). Check the label on yours. A BW Clip runs non-stop once activated, for 2 or 3 years by model; the 2-year H2S and CO models can be paused in a hibernation case (BW CLIP).
test: Bump it before each day's use: a short shot of H2S test gas above the alarm points must set off the horn, lights and vibration (OSHA SHIB). MSA's single-gas unit takes 40 ppm H2S and shows OK or ERR; an ERR or a failed alarm test means take it out of service (MSA ALTAIR SINGLE). A bump checks response, not accuracy; calibration with certified gas does that, and H2S test gas is stable only for a limited time, so never use an expired cylinder (OSHA SHIB). Without test gas there is no way to prove an H2S sensor works: in clean air a live sensor and a dead one both read zero (ISC BUMP). Other checks on a found unit: it passes its self-test (a BW Clip checks battery, sensor and electronics once a day) (BW CLIP); the remaining run time, where shown; no battery or end-of-life warning; a recent calibration or bump date. A BW Clip's warranty covers 2 or 3 years from activation plus a year on the shelf before activation (BW CLIP), so a never-activated one older than that is suspect. After a big exposure, let it recover in fresh air; if the reading won't settle back to zero, it needs recalibrating (MSA 4XR). Treat an unbumped H2S monitor as a maybe, not an all-clear.

decay.note: A BW Clip is rated for 2 or 3 years from activation, plus a year on the shelf before it (BW CLIP). Electrochemical cells commonly last 2 to 3 years (MSA BLOG FIXED), and Industrial Scientific says H2S sensors typically last over 4 (ISC O2 LIFE). H2S test gas goes stale (OSHA SHIB).

improvise: A bump-tested 4-gas monitor with an H2S sensor does this job and also covers oxygen and flammable gas. A single-gas O2 or CO monitor is no stand-in: each sensor reads its own gas, and MSA's CO sensor reads 0 ppm in 40 ppm H2S (MSA 4XR). Your nose is a warning only at low levels: smell is lost at 100 to 150 ppm, so a rotten-egg smell that fades means danger, not relief (OSHA H2S). H2S collects in low-lying areas and confined spaces (CCOHS H2S). With no proven monitor, treat sewers, septic tanks, manure pits, lift stations, sour wells and tank hatches as deadly: stay out of them and out of low ground beside them, and work from outside. Spaces should be tested before entry and monitored the whole time, and more than 60% of confined-space deaths are would-be rescuers, so never go in after someone who collapsed (NIOSH 86-110). The oil-tank deaths in the CDC study came from hydrocarbon vapour and low oxygen with H2S ruled out, and an H2S sensor doesn't measure either (MMWR TANKS, MSA 4XR). Useless: an unbumped monitor sitting at 0 ppm, which may be dead (ISC BUMP).

buildings.loc: Wastewater lift stations, headworks building and operators' trucks
Safety office or gate-house gear rack at pulp, food and chemical plants
Hazmat or rescue kit on the trucks
Landfill office and leachate pump station
Hog or dairy barn office near the manure pit
